stem: The broadcast repeatedly blames 'your superiors' for sending GIs to die in a hopeless attack. What psychological tactic is this?
stimulus: Paraphrase of a Japanese WWII English-language radio broadcast to American troops: Hello, Yankee brothers. This is your Japanese sister, the Voice of Truth. This morning your superiors are sending you to attempt the impossible, for you cannot dislodge our forces. I am filled with sadness for you, thinking of the thousands of Japanese soldiers safe in caves and pillboxes your bombs cannot touch, reluctantly waiting to slaughter you. They bear you no ill will; they know what you attempt is futile. Why die for people who sit snug and secure 11,000 miles away?
options: (A) Praising American commanders for their brilliant leadership and tactical genius in battle
(B) Driving a wedge between soldiers and their officers to erode discipline

(D) Teaching infantry tactics
explanation: By blaming 'your superiors' for ordering a hopeless attack, the broadcast invites GIs to see their own officers, not the Japanese, as the enemy. Turning soldiers against their command corrodes the discipline armies need to fight.

stimulus: Paraphrase of Dennis Brutus's 1973 poem on Sharpeville (1960): Black South Africans gathered unarmed before police stations to protest the pass laws, and at Sharpeville police fired into the crowd. stimulus: Mexican broadside, 19th century: '¡Viva el cura Hidalgo! Una página de gloria' ('Long live Father Hidalgo! A page of glory'). An oval portrait shows Miguel Hidalgo, the parish priest of Dolores, in clerical dress; the text celebrates his September 1810 uprising for Mexican independence.

stem: A historian claims that Watt's engine was a key enabling technology of the Industrial Revolution. Which evidence best supports this claim?
stimulus: Technical diagram of a Watt steam engine, c. 1780 (from an 1878 engineering history). Labeled parts show the cylinder, the great overhead beam, the flywheel, and the centrifugal governor that regulated its speed — the rotary-motion engine able to drive mill machinery anywhere, not only beside water or a coal mine.
options: (A) The engine provided reliable rotary power independent of water or wind, letting factories locate in cities near workers and markets
(B) The engine was immediately used to build steam railroads across every continent in the 1770s, decades before Stephenson, even in Asia

(D) The engine was powered by electricity, the era's newest energy source
explanation: Earlier power sources tied mills to fast rivers. A fuel-efficient steam engine freed factory location, which is why Manchester and Birmingham could grow around coal and labor rather than waterfalls. Watt's rotary-motion engine — cylinder, beam, and flywheel driving mill machinery anywhere — is exactly this location-independent power source.

stem: The two cases together best support which of the following connections about decolonization?
stimulus: India won independence from Britain in 1947 after mass campaigns and negotiations, though partition created Pakistan amid terrible violence. A decade later Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah's mass movement, became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence — an achievement celebrated across the continent as proof that colonial rule could be ended.
options: (A) Decolonization occurred only in Africa.
(B) Both independence movements used exactly the same strategies, negotiated identical settlements with Britain, and achieved exactly the same results in the very same year without any differences.
(C) Britain granted independence to all of its colonies at the same time.

explanation: The passage deliberately contrasts two routes to independence — India's negotiated transfer with mass campaigns, and Ghana's movement-led victory a decade later — and notes Ghana's inspirational effect. Decolonization was one broad wave but not one single method.

stem: Which of the following is the best-supported argument about the reforms described in the stimulus?
stimulus: In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union. His glasnost (openness) allowed freer speech and a freer press; his perestroika (restructuring) introduced limited private enterprise to revive a stagnant economy. The reforms were meant to strengthen socialism. Instead, newly free media exposed decades of failure, and nationalist movements in the Baltic republics and Central Asia demanded independence. explanation: The stimulus stresses that Gorbachev intended to strengthen socialism, yet glasnost's exposure of failure and the nationalist mobilization it enabled destroyed the system's legitimacy instead. stimulus: A Soviet World War II poster shows a young soldier and a young woman worker standing shoulder to shoulder beneath a red banner. The caption reads: 'Young men and women, defend the freedom, the motherland, and the honor that was won by your fathers.'

skill.recheck_rationale: Stem asks which broader twentieth-century development the anti-apartheid struggle belongs to; the student identifies the development (anti-colonial movements for self-determination). Topic is decoloni

stem: The struggle against apartheid described in the passage belongs to which of the following broader twentieth-century developments?
stimulus: In 1960, the township of Sharpeville became a symbol of South Africa's racial order. Under the apartheid laws, every Black South African man was required to carry a passbook, a small document recording where he was permitted to live and work. To be found in a city without the proper stamp meant arrest. On March 21, thousands of Black protesters gathered outside the Sharpeville police station, deliberately leaving their passbooks at home in a planned act of defiance. The police opened fire on the unarmed crowd, killing sixty-nine people, most of them shot in the back as they fled. The government's response was not reform but repression: the African National Congress and its rivals were banned, and leaders such as Nelson Mandela were driven underground and then imprisoned. For the white minority that held all political power, the massacre confirmed the need for ever harsher control. For Black South Africans, it proved that peaceful protest alone would not end a system that denied them citizenship in their own country. Sharpeville drew the world's attention to apartheid and pushed the liberation movement toward armed resistance. Four years later, Mandela stood trial for his life at Rivonia, using the courtroom to indict apartheid before the world. Although the regime survived for three more decades, Sharpeville marked the moment when South Africa's racial order became an international scandal rather than a domestic arrangement.
options: (A) The expansion of European colonial empires in Africa and Asia
(B) Anti-colonial movements fighting for self-determination
(C) The rise of fascist movements in Europe in the 1930s
(D) The spread of absolute monarchies across the globe
explanation: The anti-apartheid struggle was part of the great twentieth-century wave in which colonized and racially oppressed peoples demanded freedom: African and Asian decolonization, the American civil rights movement, and campaigns against white-minority rule in Rhodesia and South Africa. Though South Africa was formally independent, its Black majority lived under a system the world increasingly judged as colonial in character.

stem: Musa's account of copper being carried south and exchanged for gold at two-thirds its weight most directly illustrates which of the following?
stimulus: A traveler reported what Sultan Musa of Mali told him: at a certain town the sultan has a copper mine, from which ingots are carried to another town. 'There is nothing in my kingdom,' Musa said, 'on which a duty is levied except this crude copper that is brought in. Duty is collected on this and on nothing else. We send it to the land of the pagan Sudan and sell it for two-thirds of its weight in gold, so that we sell a hundred measures of copper for sixty-six and two-thirds measures of gold.' He added that there are pagan peoples in his kingdom from whom he does not collect the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, but whom he simply employs in extracting gold from its deposits. The gold is dug from pits about a man's height in depth, found embedded in the sides of the pits or gathered at the bottom. — Al-Umari, Arab historian, writing about 1340
options: (A) The trans-Saharan trade, in which West African gold was exchanged for goods brought from the north.
(B) Mali's military conquest of North African cities.
(C) Direct European control of West African mines through heavily fortified coastal trading forts in the 1300s.
(D) The collapse of the West African gold trade by 1340.
explanation: The passage describes a working exchange circuit — northern copper traded southward for Sudanese gold at a stated rate — the classic trans-Saharan pattern by which Mali's wealth moved across the desert.

stem: Columbus's description of the islanders as 'destitute of arms' and 'timid and full of terror' most directly foreshadows which of the following?
stimulus: On the island called Hispana there are very lofty and beautiful mountains, rich farms, groves, and fields, most fertile both for cultivation and for pasturage, and well suited for building. The harbors of this island, and the excellence of its rivers in volume and wholesomeness, surpass human belief unless one sees them. Its trees, pasturelands, and fruits differ greatly from those of Juana. Moreover, this Hispana abounds in various kinds of spices, gold, and metals. The inhabitants, as I said before, are unprovided with any sort of iron; they are destitute of arms, which are entirely unknown to them and unsuited to them — not on account of any bodily deformity, for they are well made, but because they are timid and full of terror. — Christopher Columbus, report of his first voyage, 1493
options: (A) Spanish arguments that conquest would be easy because the native population could not resist.
(B) Spanish adoption of native Caribbean military tactics.
(C) Columbus's secret plan to arm the islanders as military allies in a future war against the rival Portuguese.
(D) A Spanish decision to avoid the island entirely.
explanation: By stressing that the islanders lacked iron weapons and were fearful, Columbus signaled to his royal audience that the island could be taken with little risk — the premise of the conquest that followed.

stem: Which of the following groups' interests are most clearly ignored by the treaty's division of the world between Spain and Portugal?
stimulus: To settle the controversy between their sovereigns over which lands, among all those discovered in the ocean sea up to the present day, belong to each side, and for the sake of peace and concord and the preservation of the love between the King of Portugal and the King and Queen of Castile and Aragon, their representatives have covenanted and agreed as follows. A boundary — a straight line — shall be determined and drawn north and south, from pole to pole, across the said ocean sea, from the Arctic to the Antarctic pole. This line shall be drawn straight at a distance of 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, calculated by degrees or by whatever method is judged best and readiest, provided the distance is no greater than stated. All lands, both islands and mainlands, already found and discovered, or to be found and discovered hereafter, lying on the eastern side of this line — whether reached by the King of Portugal or by his vessels — in either north or south latitude, provided the said line is not crossed, shall belong to, and remain forever in the possession of, the King of Portugal and his successors. And all other lands, both islands and mainlands, already found or to be found hereafter, discovered or to be discovered hereafter by the King and Queen of Castile and Aragon or by their vessels, lying on the western side of this line after passing it toward the west, in either north or south latitude, shall belong to, and remain forever in the possession of, the King and Queen of Castile and Leon and their successors. — Treaty of Tordesillas between Spain and Portugal, 1494
options: (A) Spanish merchants seeking new markets.
(B) Portuguese navigators exploring the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
(C) The papacy, which brokered the agreement.
(D) The Indigenous peoples whose lands were divided.
explanation: The treaty carves up entire continents between two European crowns without any reference to the peoples already living there — their sovereignty is simply assumed away.

stem: During the 1857 uprising, rebel sepoys rallied around the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar in Delhi. This decision most directly demonstrates which of the following?
stimulus: Sunday, the 10th of May, dawned in peace and happiness. The early morning service at the cantonment church saw many assembled together, some never to meet on earth again. The day passed in quiet happiness; no thought of danger disturbed the serenity of that happy home. How differently closed the Sabbath that had dawned so tranquilly! We were on the point of going to the evening service when the disturbance commenced on the native parade ground. Shots and volumes of smoke told of what was going on: our servants begged us not to show ourselves and urged the necessity of closing our doors, as the mob was approaching. My husband, after loading his arms, took me to the terrace on top of the house; two of our countrywomen also took refuge with us to escape the rebels' bullets. Just at this moment an officer of the 3rd Cavalry galloped up at full speed, having dashed through the mutinous troops, fired at on all sides, to give us notice of the danger. — Elisa Greathed, a British resident of Meerut, describing the outbreak of the Indian uprising, May 1857
options: (A) The emperor's personal command of rebel military operations.
(B) The Mughal dynasty's symbolic authority as a focus of anti-British resistance.
(C) British support for restoring full Mughal power.
(D) The emperor's success in converting the sepoys to a new religion of his own making.
explanation: The aged, powerless emperor was proclaimed leader because the Mughal name still carried legitimacy — rebels needed a symbol around which Hindus and Muslims could unite against the British.

stem: Several major trading cities on the map, such as Timbuktu and the Hausa city-states, lie far from any ocean coast. What does their prosperity best demonstrate about African trade networks in this period?
stimulus: Map: African trade centers, c. 1250-1600. In West Africa: the Ghana region, the Mali Empire (c. 1230s-1400s) with Timbuktu and the Hausa city-states, and the Songhai Empire (1460s-1591). The Sahara Desert lies to the north, crossed by caravan routes linking the Sahel to Mediterranean ports. In East and southern Africa: the Swahili city-states (1400s), including Mogadishu, Kilwa, and Sofala on the Indian Ocean coast, and Great Zimbabwe (1300s-1400s) in the interior. Also shown: the Red Sea, the Nile River, the Zambezi and Limpopo Rivers, and the Kalahari Desert. Trade routes connect gold-producing interior regions to both Saharan and Indian Ocean outlets.
options: (A) Only cities on the Nile River could support large populations.
(B) Interior cities grew wealthy by deliberately cutting off all contact with foreign merchants and caravans.
(C) Coastal trade was unimportant compared with the Saharan trade.
(D) Inland cities could prosper when connected to long-distance caravan routes.
explanation: Cities like Timbuktu sat at the southern end of trans-Saharan caravan routes. Their wealth shows that prosperity depended on connection to trade routes, not on being located on the coast.
